Messages.Author: Matt Guinn
Messages.Body:
I have decided to stop lurking and contribute to this wonderful
resource.
Virgin poster, be nice.

The majority of VEKN rules are set up to maintain the predator-prey
relationship, and at the same time requiring players to play to win.
However, I find that there are very few instances where a judge could
over-rule a play made by a player. In fact, the only question a judge
could ask would be, "Are you playing to win?". This is because the
judge can't possibly have as much knowledge about the game as the
player.

If an action were to be disallowed how do you resolve a player leaving
the table?

Rules are set up to govern an event of game, while floor rules are an
extension of those and should outline consquences should those be
violated.

I believe that the rules reguarding play-to-win are currently
un-enforcable.
No action can be prohibited if a player "says" she is playing to win.

Player may also make statements as to the motivations of their actions
that are untrue, in order influence the game. It may be in someones
interest to put another player on "tilt" by suggesting their
motivations are for out of game reasons. This kind of legal play
merely muddies the water when discussing the play in question.

Further, a player can say she can not win, or get additional VPs, and
thus may lose as they choose- allowing whatever play they wish. Do we
need the lose as you choose clause? Does the game benifit from this
cop-out, or would we be better to insist people play to win for the
entire game? We can't regulate proper play, but by allowing this out
players can justify any action they wish to take.

In addition it has been ruled that prize support may be taken into
account for deals, self ousting or whatever. This ruling must be
reversed, how is prize support any different from cash, favors, hes my
buddy, I want to get a ride home cause he brought me here. If
anything outside the game, prize support, is introduced as a legal
consideration for in game decisions then the line is blurred.

It is interesting that prize support can be considered for play, but
tournament position is not allowed to be considered. I can't make
deal for one VP that gets me into the finals, but I an give a guy half
my box of boosters to roll for me.

Luckily the lastest batch of prize support was such crap that no-one
wanted it and thus deals were not an issue.

Would like to here specific instances of judges over-ruling actions,
or other pertinent ruling in the past that may not have been posted.

Thanks for the time,

Matt

When is VTES con? Do we need to pay $60 for badges when to only thing
we are going to do is play cards?

You are imagining that the judge has to prove he's right in order to take
action. He doesn't, anymore than a real judge needs omniscience to
act. They're called "judges", not "logicians".

> If an action were to be disallowed how do you resolve a player leaving
> the table?

You wing it. Feel free to propose guidelines; I'd like some, even though
I've never actually had to deal with this.

> Rules are set up to govern an event of game,

You've been in the Buckminster Fuller again, haven't you? ;)

> while floor rules are an
> extension of those and should outline consquences should those be
> violated.

I guess you're talking about rules vs. tournament rules here, but I'm not
sure.

> I believe that the rules reguarding play-to-win are currently
> un-enforcable.

They are enforcable, but not in the agent-less way that you would seem to
like. I mean, I would like it too, since it's much easier to say "2 + 2
= 4, so you're out" than it is to look someone in the eye and say "It's my
belief that you are a fuckhead, so leave my game." I take great comfort
in the fact that this has never actually been an issue for me, so I don't
worry about it much.

> No action can be prohibited if a player "says" she is playing to win.

Sure it can, watch: "I prohibit you." See? I'm kind of joking around,
sure, but the point I'm making is serious: you can't remove the
"judgement" from judging. Sometimes judges are wrong. In the real world,
sometimes people die because judges are wrong, but we don't forego a legal
system for lack of perfect omniscience. It's just getting by with the
best that's humanly possible. A Jyhad tournament is no different.

I don't see the benefit of "lose as you choose", however. If there is a
benefit, I believe the drawbacks outweigh it. Matt and I both have some
personal experience with some extreme "lose as you choose", though, so we
may be biased. I can't recall it actually spoiling any tournament games
I've played in or judged, though.

> Luckily the lastest batch of prize support was such crap that no-one

The demise of prize-support-that's-worth-a-damn may be a good thing,

months in advance, but at the same time wanting free stuff to give out as
compensation for people leaving their house-wombs. If I can get people
used to paying $5 to play, we could be doing tournaments right and left.

Well, there was this one guy I gave a warning to for stalling one

"Matt Guinn" <wm...@mail.com> wrote in message

> I have decided to stop lurking and contribute to this wonderful

> over-rule a play made by a player. In fact, the only question a judge
> could ask would be, "Are you playing to win?". This is because the
> judge can't possibly have as much knowledge about the game as the
> player.

Yeah, as David and LSJ have pointed out, the judge can do
what he or she wants. They don't have to prove that they're
right. It definitely could get sticky if they want to keep
a player in the game while not allowing the player to play
as he/she wants, though.

> If an action were to be disallowed how do you resolve a player leaving
> the table?

That's up to the judge. No one said judging was easy. :-)

You might leave a "null player" in that position, with pool
but no other permanents, or remove the position entirely
with no award of VP or pool, or something else.

> Rules are set up to govern an event of game, while floor rules are an
> extension of those and should outline consquences should those be
> violated.
>
> I believe that the rules reguarding play-to-win are currently
> un-enforcable.
> No action can be prohibited if a player "says" she is playing to win.

It can, but prohibiting a player's actions may not make the
player any more cooperative, yeah.

> Player may also make statements as to the motivations of their actions
> that are untrue, in order influence the game. It may be in someones
> interest to put another player on "tilt" by suggesting their
> motivations are for out of game reasons. This kind of legal play
> merely muddies the water when discussing the play in question.

Interesting point. Given that players cannot actually legally
act on out-of-game considerations, they should perhaps refrain
from claiming that they are doing so. If the judge is called
in, the judge will have to decide whether the player is in fact
doing things for out-of-game reasons, or was lying about having
out-of-game motivation to influence the other players (waters
muddied by the possibility that they are now lying to the
judge in the claim that they were never really doing things
for out-of-game reasons).

> Further, a player can say she can not win, or get additional VPs, and
> thus may lose as they choose- allowing whatever play they wish. Do we
> need the lose as you choose clause? Does the game benifit from this
> cop-out, or would we be better to insist people play to win for the
> entire game? We can't regulate proper play, but by allowing this out
> players can justify any action they wish to take.

We do insist that players play to win for the entire game.
You must play to win as long as you have a reasonable (in
the opinion of the judge) chance of doing so. If you cannot
win, you must try to earn as many VPs as you can. You do
have the choice of earning your maximum VPs in any way that
you see fit. That's not a justification for throwing games.
It is, again, a judgement call, but in my opinion, it's
unusual for a player to have no reasonable chance of getting
any more VPs while he or she still has the resources to
substantially disrupt the game.

To me, this again points to the idea that VTES simply cannot
be played in too-competitive a fashion. You have to be able
to rely on people to be good sports and play in the spirit
of the game. If they're not willing to do this, the game
won't be fun and no amount of judging will make it fun. You
could try ejecting people for poor sportsmanship, but that's
not exactly a friendly solution or likely to make people
happy with the outcome.

> In addition it has been ruled that prize support may be taken into
> account for deals, self ousting or whatever. This ruling must be
> reversed, how is prize support any different from cash, favors, hes my
> buddy, I want to get a ride home cause he brought me here. If
> anything outside the game, prize support, is introduced as a legal
> consideration for in game decisions then the line is blurred.

It's not a ruling, it's in the VEKN tournament rules.

http://www.white-wolf.com/vtes/veknJudgesGuide.html

Section 161, Cheating - Bribery.

You're right, it's weird and probably not right. I think this
is one of those things that was carried over from the DCI
Magic tournament rules and is probably not appropriate to VTES
tournament play.

> Would like to here specific instances of judges over-ruling actions,
> or other pertinent ruling in the past that may not have been posted.

I can't off the top of my head think of any actual cases where
a judge has intervened in a game in this way. Normally the
VTES tournament games I've actually seen have had enough good
sportsmanship that it hasn't become a problem.

Anyone else have examples? It's certainly possible for it to
become a problem.

Josh

yay, new prize support system soon!

Messages.Author: salem
Messages.Body:
On 15 Oct 2003 09:49:52 -0700, kit3...@yahoo.com (Jeff Haar)
scrawled:

>wm...@mail.com (Matt Guinn) wrote in message news:<263773d7.0310...@posting.google.com>...

>> Further, a player can say she can not win, or get additional VPs, and
>> thus may lose as they choose- allowing whatever play they wish. Do we
>> need the lose as you choose clause? Does the game benifit from this
>> cop-out, or would we be better to insist people play to win for the
>> entire game? We can't regulate proper play, but by allowing this out
>> players can justify any action they wish to take.
>
>This does lead to problems. Why does a losing player deserve to
>determine anything outside of the fact that they lose?

Well, if a player is in the 'lose as you choose' state, then they are
playing to win. They are trying to get as many more vps as they can.
By definition of the state they are in, the maximum number of further
vps they can reasonably get is 0. So if they bleed with all they have,
they'll get 0 more vps. If they wall up, 0 more vps, if they rush
someone because they hate Hesha, they get 0 more vps. So, they are
free to 'lose as they choose', because no matter what they do it won't
help them get more vps. If there was some course of action that would
help them get more vps that they were aware of, then they wouldn't
actually be in the 'lose as you choose' state.

If you forced them to, say, bleed with everything they had, that would
be an advantage to their predator. By the definition of the state they
are in, they're not going to be ousting their prey (that would get
them a vp). So all they do is make the prey use up some resources, and
make it easier for their predator to clean them up. So the predator is
advataged.

If you forced them to wall up, you give their prey an advantage. The
prey gets no pressure for a bit, and the predator has to use extra
resources that could otherwise have been used on the next guy to oust
the losing player.

If you force them to act backwards, it's roughly the same effect as
above.

Whatever they do or don't do will advantage someone or other more than
if they didn't or did do the thing. No one else should be allowed to
choose for a player who they give advantage to but that player.

Assuming of course they can not reasonably expect to get any more VPs.

>> In addition it has been ruled that prize support may be taken into
>> account for deals, self ousting or whatever. This ruling must be
>> reversed, how is prize support any different from cash, favors, hes my
>> buddy, I want to get a ride home cause he brought me here. If
>> anything outside the game, prize support, is introduced as a legal
>> consideration for in game decisions then the line is blurred.

The reasoning I heard was, say in the final some guy offers you half
of first prize if you fall down for him so he comes first and you come
second, and you were the only two guys left. If you could actually
oust him and come first, you'd be getting all of first prize anyway,
so you'd never take the deal.
So accepting deals based on prizes only hurts the guy offering the
deal.

salem

Messages.Author: salem
Messages.Body:
On 15 Oct 2003 19:05:35 -0700, ira...@yahoo.com (Ira) scrawled:



If the game was likely to time out anyway, and the predator, while he
had spent a lot of resources trying to oust the leaving player, wasn't
guarantee'd of ousting him, but then again wasn't unlikely to, the
Judge might award 0.4 (or, really, anything greater than 0 and less
than 0.5), so that when the game times out they don't get a full vp
(so someone else that did oust someone, and was then ousted, is still
better off), but the 0.4 makes them better off than someone who merely
stayed in till time.

We used to have a rough house rule in social games for people who left
mid game:
Predator gets 0.5vps, and pool equal to:
Max(6 -(leaving player's remaining pool), 0)
and the leaving player was no longer part of the game as if he was
ousted.



disadvantage him.

the rule are above the judge's knowledge. There is just too much that
cannot be known to a judge.

player with no permanents and no deck and one pool vs. a minion with
blood and no pre-existing deals.

Messages.Author: the_capuchin
Messages.Body:
> The reasoning I heard was, say in the final some guy offers you half
> of first prize if you fall down for him so he comes first and you come
> second, and you were the only two guys left. If you could actually
> oust him and come first, you'd be getting all of first prize anyway,
> so you'd never take the deal.
> So accepting deals based on prizes only hurts the guy offering the
> deal.

In a final with two players left, yes. That's why i don't bother about
prize splitting as much unsportsmanlike behaviour. For me, it's
thematically appropriate for two players to agree on not attacking
each other if they fall on the same table until they are the two left,
so they can try to make it easier for the two to get VPs, fight for
the GW and split the prize. This kind of behaviour does not entirely
disrupt the table since any deck should be prepared for a predator
who's got free reign anyway - this could always happen in a "normal",
no-deal-made table. What I do hate though is a player actively
disrupting the mood - say, predator and prey are friends, play with
the same collection of cards and not only the predator does not attack
its prey, but the prey blocks/denials/disrupt anything cross-table
just to prevent its predator from being ousted with no reason other
than to guarantee that his predator friend will stay alive. I now
there are some situations where it's for the best interest - like
preventing anyone to get potencial VPs you'll need, or having a new
predator who is very likely to be capable of ousting you - but most of
these situations arise late in the game, and most judges could
snapshot them very easily.
For the record, I'm bitching a little bit since it never happened to
me until the last tournament I've played. Maybe I'll get used to it,
but I gotta say that I find VEKN rules to be most accurate and
understable. What I do not have the luck to see is competent judges
(sometimes no judges at all, just "time guardians"). If something is
to be changed, is not about prize splitting or stating what is a
"reasonable chance" to make VPs. Should be some way of enforcing
multi-judge system.

I thought your personal crusade was that a "reasonable" chance
of winning is more like 30% than 5%. ;-)

> > but I can give a guy half my box of boosters to roll for me.

>
> Assuming you and he don't violate the play to win rule, of course. I'll
> guarantee you this: I won't LET you make a deal for prizes in the finals
> when the player receiving (some of) the prizes has the ability to get more
> VPs.

Doesn't the "Cheating - Bribery" section imply that the "play
to win" rule is overridden by prize-splitting deals?

-----------------------------------------------------------------
161. Cheating - Bribery

Definition:

A player attempts to bribe an opponent into changing the results of
a game by offering inducements outside of the current game.

Example:

A player offers an opponent cash or cards to throw a game.

Philosophy:

Players in the finals of a tournament should not be considered in
violation of this rule as long as they meet the following criteria:

* No player introduces incentives outside the current game such as
cash, cards, or other items. (For example, splitting the prizes would
be acceptable.)

* All players involved in all affected games agree on the outcome.
------------------------------------------------------------------

If that doesn't mean that it's okay to agree to "change the
results of a game" based on a prize-split offer, what *does* it
mean? It can't very logically be talking about, for example,
all the players in a finals match agreeing to split the prizes
evenly regardless of how the VPs end up, because that couldn't
possibly fall under the "Cheating - Bribery" category, since
no one would be trying to alter the results of the game.

That is, if this exemption isn't about agreeing to alter the
results of the game, why is it included in the section on
what would otherwise be "Cheating - Bribery"?

Josh

I agree that if a player is playing to help his buddy purely because
he's his buddy, for no in game reason, then that's bad.

>(sometimes no judges at all, just "time guardians"). If something is

>"reasonable chance" to make VPs. Should be some way of enforcing

At each tournament you're at, ask who the head judge is.
Ask that he/she actually judge. call the judge over to ask things like
how much time is left, and maybe ask them things like 'what's the
latest text for this card again? i'm pretty sure it does X but i just
want to be sure'.
Let them know you want to play in a judged environment, not because
you're a rules nut, but because you just like to have a judge around
to catch the occasional slip up and preserve the integrity of the
game. Make it look like you want a judge around to stop yourself from
messing up, so the other players don't feel victimised. Also,
repeatedly mention the bit where penalties cannot be waived even if
all players at a table agree. Not many people seem to appreciate that,
and so if there is one dissenter he is pressured into waiving with the
rest of the table. This should not be allowed. Say things like 'i'd
love to let you get a pool for the edge during your minion phase, but
it's just not allowed. I could get cautioned for trying to let you do
it. sorry. even if we all want you to get that pool, the judge would
never let it happen......where is that judge, anyway?'

If blatant buddy-helping is still going on, or any unsportsmanlike
behaviour at all, or rules infringements with no repurcussions
('that's the 5th time you've replaced Read the Winds as soon as you've
played it. Judge! Judge? how much of your library do you want to look
at?' 'sorry...anyway, i'd better play this Inner Essence..oh look, i
drew a Horrid Form. how lucky....again...') try and find your
tournament on the vekn tournament calendar. If the head judge isn't
actually doing any judging, it might be worth mentioning your concern
to the Powers That Be, citing as many relevant details about the
tournament and the situations as possible.
